title: Cortés's March on Tenochtitlan
intro: Hernán Cortés left Cuba in 1519 against the governor's wishes with 11 ships and about 630 men, and with Indigenous allies, mainly Tlaxcalans, marched inland to Tenochtitlan, capital of the Aztec Triple Alliance ruled by Moctezuma II. The campaign ended in the siege and fall of the city in 1521.
ending: Tenochtitlan and Tlatelolco fell on 13 August 1521 and Cuauhtémoc was captured. The city was largely destroyed and Mexico City was built on its ruins as the capital of New Spain; the surviving Mexica were forbidden to live in Tenochtitlan.

legs.title: From Cuba to the Gulf coast

stops.text: Governor Velázquez came to the dock at Santiago de Cuba and sent orders to hold the fleet and arrest Cortés. Cortés sailed for Trinidad regardless, beginning the expedition with the legal status of a mutineer.
stops.quote: Velázquez then sent orders for the fleet to be held and Cortés taken prisoner. Nevertheless, Cortés set sail, beginning his expedition with the legal status of a mutineer.

stops.text: Cortés spent some time on the island trying to convert the locals to Christianity, with mixed results. He heard of Spaniards living in Yucatán, and the shipwreck survivor Gerónimo de Aguilar joined him as a translator.
stops.quote: Cortés spent some time at the island of Cozumel, on the east coast of Yucatán, trying to convert the locals to Christianity, something that provided mixed results. While at Cozumel, Cortés heard reports of other white men living in the Yucatán.

stops.text: Cortés defeated the local people in two battles. Their leaders then sued for peace and gave the Spaniards 20 enslaved women, among them the Nahua woman later known as Doña Marina or La Malinche, who became a main translator.
stops.quote: Cortés continued round the tip of the Yucatán Peninsula and landed at Potonchán, where there was little gold. After defeating the local natives in two battles

stops.text: The expedition landed on the Gulf coast near San Juan de Ulúa. Cortés was welcomed by representatives of Moctezuma II and tried to frighten them with a display of firepower.
stops.quote: 21 April – Expedition lands in the Gulf coast near San Juan de Ullúa

stops.text: Cortés persuaded the Totonac chiefs to rebel against the Aztecs, and five of Moctezuma's tax collectors were taken prisoner. The Totonacs helped build Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz, the starting point of the campaign.
stops.quote: Cortés quickly persuaded the Totonac chiefs to rebel against the Aztecs, taking prisoner five of Moctezuma's tax collectors.

stops.text: The Otomi and Tlaxcalans first fought the Spanish in three battles from 2 to 5 September, then allied with them against the Aztecs. Cortés stayed twenty days, and the Tlaxcalans became his most important allies.
stops.quote: On 23 September 1519, Cortés arrived in Tlaxcala and was greeted with joy by the rulers, who saw the Spanish as an ally against the Aztecs.

stops.text: The Spaniards, helped by Tlaxcalans, massacred the people of Cholula and burned the city. Cortés claimed 3,000 dead and Vázquez de Tapia as many as 30,000, though many had fled. Accounts differ on the cause.
stops.quote: In letters to his King, Cortés claimed that in three hours time his troops (helped by the Tlaxcalans) killed 3,000 people and had burned the city. Another witness, Vázquez de Tapia, claimed the death toll was as high as 30,000.

stops.text: Cortés and his forces entered the island capital, where Moctezuma met them on the causeway. By 14 November Moctezuma was Cortés's prisoner, though modern scholars doubt Cortés's own claim about when he took him.
stops.quote: On 8 November 1519, after the fall of Cholula, Cortés and his forces entered Tenochtitlan, the island capital of the Mexica-Aztecs.

stops.text: Governor Velázquez had sent Pánfilo de Narváez to seize Cortés. Cortés attacked at night, wounded and captured him, and won over most of his men with promises of riches and commands.
stops.quote: Cortés set out against Narváez, who had advanced onto Cempoala. Cortés surprised his antagonist with a night attack, during which his men wounded Narváez in the eye and took him prisoner.

stops.text: Cortés found that Alvarado had attacked and killed many Aztec nobles at a religious festival in the Great Temple. Alvarado said he feared an attack. The city rose, and Moctezuma died, the Aztecs saying the Spaniards killed him.
stops.quote: When Cortés returned to Tenochtitlan in late May, he found that Alvarado and his men had attacked and killed many of the Aztec nobility in the Massacre in the Great Temple, that happened during a religious festival organized by the Aztecs.

stops.text: The Spaniards and their allies fled along the causeway at night and were attacked from the causeway and from canoes. Losses were put at 860 Spanish soldiers, 72 other Spaniards and 1,000 Tlaxcalan warriors.
stops.quote: On the rainy night of 10 July 1520, the Spaniards and their allies set out for the mainland via the causeway to Tlacopan.

stops.text: The Aztecs tried to destroy the retreating Spanish at the Battle of Otumba. The infantry held while the cavalry charged repeatedly, and the Aztecs left the field after Cortés's men killed one of their leaders.
stops.quote: On 14 July 1520, the Aztecs attempted to destroy the Spanish for good at the Battle of Otumba.

stops.text: The 440 surviving Spaniards, all wounded and with only 20 horses left, found refuge among the Tlaxcalans. Smallpox struck the Aztecs from September, and killed the new emperor Cuitláhuac on 4 December, perhaps of the disease.
stops.quote: The Spanish were able to complete their escape to Tlaxcala. There, they were given assistance, since all 440 of them were wounded, with only 20 horses left.

stops.text: Spanish, Tlaxcalan and Texcocan forces made Texcoco their base against Tenochtitlan. In April Tlaxcalan labourers built 13 shallow-bottomed brigantines under Spanish supervision, giving the allies control of Lake Texcoco.
stops.quote: February – Combined Spanish-Tlaxcalteca-Texcoca forces attack Xaltocan and Tlacopan; Texcoco becomes the base of operations for the campaign against Tenochtitlan

stops.text: The siege began and cut off the drinking water from Chapultepec. The causeways were cut and the lake was held by armed brigantines. The defenders under Cuauhtémoc refused every offer to end it.
stops.quote: 10 May – Start of the siege of Tenochtitlan; potable water from Chapultepec cut off

stops.text: Tenochtitlan and Tlatelolco fell and Cuauhtémoc was captured trying to flee by canoe. Sacking and violence against the survivors followed from 13 to 17 August. The city was almost totally destroyed.
stops.quote: Tenochtitlan and Tlatelolco fell on 13 August 1521, during which the Emperor was captured trying to escape the city in a canoe.

notes: Source is the article on the conquest of the Aztec Empire, so the route is Cortés's. Contradictions: the article dates the retreat 10 July (text) and 30 June (timeline), Otumba 14 July (text) and 7 July (timeline), and Cortés's return to Tenochtitlan 'late May' and 'St. John's Day June 1520' (24 June in timeline); I used the running text and 'June 1520'. Casualty figures differ too (860 soldiers + 72 others + 1,000 Tlaxcalans in text; perhaps 1,000 each in timeline). The siege 'eight months' (text) conflicts with 10 May to 13 August (timeline); the stop avoids the figure. Smallpox (killing 5-8 million in 1520, per the intro) is told in the Tlaxcala stop text only briefly; the article places it in Tenochtitlan. Left out: Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz and the scuttling of the ships (no named place the map can point to; the article gives no firm location), Tepeaca (timeline only), Tlatelolco, Tlacopan 1521 attack. Trinidad (Cuba): the article gives the departure as 10 February 1519 only in the timeline, so the date is 'February 1519'. Potonchán: the date 24 March is from the timeline's 'Potoncan' line, not quoted. Check wp titles: Potonchán, Cempoala, Texcoco de Mora, Otumba de Gómez Farías, Cholula, Puebla. places.tsv has veracruz-city and mexico-city but they are not these places; Texcoco entry is only the lake.
